planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Palisade is a narrow, upright selection bred for tight urban planting strips where the wide-spreading species habit won't fit.

directions: Palisade holds a dense, uniformly narrow, upright silhouette from a young age, sparing it the slow, irregular spreading habit typical of seedling American hornbeam and making it far more predictable as a specimen or streetscape tree in confined spaces. Grow it in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil with partial to full shade, matching the woodland-edge conditions the species favors in the wild; it also tolerates the compacted, reflected-heat conditions of urban planters better than the species type. The smooth, sinewy gray bark and clean fall color are unchanged from the species, so it delivers the same ornamental interest in a fraction of the footprint. Established trees need little supplemental care beyond occasional watering during drought.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery introduction notes

common_name: Fastigiata European Hornbeam (Columnar Street Tree Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun to partial shade; Fastigiata starts as a tight, narrow cone and gradually broadens into an oval crown with age.

directions: Fastigiata is the long-established, classic columnar selection of European hornbeam, historically among the most widely planted street trees in European cities for its predictable, formal, upright-oval habit and tolerance of pollution, compacted soils, and root restriction. It retains the same dense, twiggy branching and winter marcescence (persistent tan leaves) that make the species so valuable for hedging, though Fastigiata's habit widens noticeably with age rather than staying columnar for life, so allow room for the crown to fill out at maturity. It adapts to a wide range of soils including heavy clay and tolerates urban heat and reflected light well. Little pruning is required beyond removing crossing branches while the tree is young to reinforce a single leader.

common_name: Frans Fontaine European Hornbeam (Narrow Uniform Columnar Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun to partial shade; Frans Fontaine keeps a noticeably narrower, more uniform columnar profile than older selections like Fastigiata even at full maturity.

directions: Frans Fontaine is a Dutch-origin selection prized for holding a tighter, more consistently narrow columnar shape than older European hornbeam cultivars, making it a favorite for formal allees, tight side-yard screens, and street tree plantings where lateral space is limited. Like the species it retains dried tan leaves through winter, giving structure and a degree of privacy screening even in the dormant season, and it shares the same tolerance for clay soil, urban pollution, and root-zone compaction. Give it well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and expect slow, steady growth with minimal pruning needed to maintain its naturally uniform habit. It is an excellent substitute for narrow conifers or fastigiate oaks in formal garden design.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant grafted nursery transplants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to slightly acidic soil in full sun; Espresso is a male clone that never produces the species' large, messy, toxic seed pods.

directions: Espresso is a male-only clone selected to eliminate the large, persistent seed pods that make the straight species messy near patios, walkways, and parking areas, while keeping all of the ornamental value of Kentucky coffeetree: the bold, doubly-pinnate leaves, the dramatic coarse winter silhouette, and the deeply furrowed gray bark. It also tends toward a somewhat more symmetrical, rounded-to-oval crown than the often gawky, irregular habit of seedling trees, making it more predictable for street and shade tree use. Like the species it is extremely drought- and pollution-tolerant once established and adapts to a wide range of soils, from moist bottomland loam to compacted urban fill. Stake young grafted trees for the first year or two until the root system anchors them.

common_name: Prairie Titan Kentucky Coffeetree (Seedless Male Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted nursery transplants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to slightly acidic soil in full sun; Prairie Titan is a seedless male selection bred for a more uniform, upright-pyramidal habit than seedling trees.

directions: Prairie Titan was selected for a more upright, pyramidal-to-oval crown and stronger central leader than the often sparse, irregular branching of seedling-grown Kentucky coffeetree, giving nurseries and municipalities a more predictably shaped shade tree for street and boulevard plantings. As a male clone it never sets the large, tough seed pods that litter sidewalks under the species, while retaining the huge, doubly-pinnate leaves and bold winter branch structure that make the species so distinctive. It shares the species' outstanding drought, heat, and pollution tolerance and adapts to a broad range of soils once its taproot is established, though staking during the first couple of seasons helps it establish a straight leader. Prune only to remove competing leaders while young; mature trees need little maintenance.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America
